docs.title: esbi-cli documentation
docs.text: esbi-cli (sb) turns the PDFs, links and emails you save into a Markdown wiki of notes, written by a local or cloud language model. These pages show how to install it, use it, and look things up. The notes it writes are in the language you choose (English or Spanish); the documentation and the command line are in English.

docs.text:
• Learn is a guided path with every output shown.
  • Do is one recipe per task.
  • Look up is complete and exact: commands, settings, files.
  • Understand explains why, with measurements where they exist.

Version 0.x: it works and is used daily, but commands and the config format can still change between minor versions; see the changelog. Released under the MIT license. Source and issues: GitHub.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: esbi-cli is a modular monolith (one Python package, one process) organised as ports and adapters (hexagonal): the logic that decides what a note says sits in the middle, and everything that touches the outside world (a model, the network, a mailbox, the Keychain, launchd, the disk) sits behind a small seam that tests replace with a fake. This page says what that means in this code, and why; for the data flow and the file layout see Internals.

docs.title: The one principle that shapes everything
docs.text: The model never touches files and never needs tool calling. The worker retrieves candidate pages, asks the model for a JSON edit plan, validates it against a schema, checks what it claims against the source, and only then writes. So the model is an adapter that turns text into validated data, and nothing else. That is what lets small local models work: they only have to produce JSON, not drive tools.

docs.title: Core, ports, adapters
docs.text:
What it is Where Core Ingest (read, plan, apply), consolidated summaries, the retrieval and ask logic, the queue and run loop, the daily index, lint, privacy rules, the machine-readable output, signal handling ingest/ (including consolidate.py), ask/, run.py, queue.py, report/, lint/, privacy.py, vault.py, index.py, jsonout.py, interrupts.py Ports The few things the core needs from outside, written as a small protocol or as a callable passed in LLM (complete_json, tokens_used, sends_text_out), MailClient, the extractor callable, ingest_fn and on_event in run_queue, the launchctl runner, the DNS resolver, the Keychain backend Adapters The real implementations llm/adapter.py (Ollama, LM Studio, OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, the claude tool, the codex tool, embeddings, OCR), ocr_models.py (which vision models exist, what each needs, and whether the local Ollama has one), mail/imap.py, extract/ (web, PDF, image, clip), netguard.py, mail/credentials.py (Keychain, or the system keyring off macOS), schedule.py (launchd), gitops.py

The dependency rule: the core depends on the ports (today the LLM protocol and its errors live in llm/adapter.py, next to the adapters) and never builds or imports a concrete provider. The CLI (cli.py) is the composition root that builds the adapters from the config (make_llm, make_embedder, make_ocr, make_mail_client) and hands them in. One known leak: the ingest pipeline asks mail/fetch.py whether a file came from email (is_mail_file, called is_mail_pdf before images were kept too), because the privacy rules need that fact. The vault is the one place the core touches the disk directly, because the vault is the product: plain Markdown files you own.

The ports are plain Python protocols and injected callables, not abstract base classes: nothing in this project needs a class hierarchy to express "a thing that returns JSON for a prompt".

docs.title: Modules that carry a rule
docs.text:
Four modules exist for one rule each, and the rest of the code goes through them.

  • interrupts.py: a signal stops a run only where that is safe. SIGINT and SIGTERM are turned into an exception in the main thread, but only inside handling(), and a signal raises (Interrupted) only inside an interruptible() block. Anything that writes more than one file wraps the writing in deferred(): a signal that arrives there waits until the block ends, so a source note, the concept pages it touched and the log line are written whole or not at all. run_queue makes the call to the model interruptible() and puts the item back in the queue without counting an attempt; sb ingest and sb reingest use exit_when_interrupted(), which exits with 128 plus the signal number. Interrupted derives from BaseException, like KeyboardInterrupt, so an except Exception meant for a failed source cannot swallow it.
  • jsonout.py: the one place that knows a machine-readable shape. Commands with --json call a function in it (jsonout.status(...), jsonout.event(...), jsonout.fail(...)) and never build a dict themselves, so the contract can be read, and tested, in one file. It also owns the contract number (additive change: same number; breaking change: bump) and only_events(), which drops the human lines from stdout during sb run --json so stdout carries events and nothing else. run_queue(on_event=...) is its port: the loop reports started, source_started, source_failed through a callback and the CLI adds the rest, so the loop has no idea what JSON is.
  • ingest/consolidate.py: summaries from evidence, checked before they are written. It builds the ## Summary of a concept page from the page's own From sections only (never the sources), checks the answer against those sections (size, markup, language, nothing stated that they do not say), retries once, and otherwise writes a note to wiki/review/ and leaves the page as it was. It is also where the privacy rule applies: a page that email helped write is summarised only by a model that runs on this machine. sb consolidate and the automatic pass (consolidate_due, capped by [run].max_consolidations_per_run) both call it.
  • The mail-link origin and ingest(from_email=...). A link found in a mail is queued with the origin mail-link; run passes from_email=True to the ingest of any queue item with that origin, and the pipeline then marks the source kind: email, so everything downstream (the private model, the hidden-from-cloud pages) treats a page reached through a mail as email. The same reason makes .esbi/mail-pdfs.txt hold the hash of every attachment saved from a mail, images included.

docs.title: Why every external effect is behind a seam
docs.text: Because tests never touch the network, a real model, the Keychain or launchd. They fake at the seams and nowhere else: a FakeLLM that returns queued JSON, a fake mail client, a fake launchctl, a resolver that returns chosen addresses, a fake Keychain backend. A new adapter or a new effect gets its seam first and its fake second; code that reaches the outside world without a seam cannot be tested and does not get merged.

docs.title: Patterns that earn their place
docs.text:
• Adapter: one per model provider and per source type, chosen by a prefix in the config (ollama/…, claude-cli/…).
  • Facade: Vault hides the layout of the folders and the page index behind a few methods.
  • Repository: Queue (SQLite) is the only owner of the work queue state.
  • Composition root: cli.py wires the parts; no module builds its own collaborators.

Patterns are not added for their own sake: a layer or an interface that has one implementation and no seam to fake is not worth having.

docs.title: Rules the design holds to
docs.text:
• KISS and YAGNI: the smallest change that works; a setting needs a reason to exist.
  • Separation of concerns: extracting text, planning, applying and reporting are separate steps with separate tests.
  • DRY, without forcing it: one source of truth for a fact (for example the language labels live in lang.py; the privacy decision lives in privacy.py).
  • Safe by default: email never reaches a model that sends text away; fetching goes through netguard.safe_get only; secrets live in the Keychain.

docs.title: Gotchas for developers
docs.text:
• iCloud and .venv. In an iCloud-synced folder (~/Documents), macOS flags files inside dot-folders as hidden and Python 3.13 then skips hidden .pth files, so import esbi_cli fails. Keep the environment outside, with UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT.
  • One writer at a time. RunLock is an flock, so a crashed run can never leave a stuck lock. The order in a run is: lock, then the "is it due" check, then build the model.
  • One way to fetch. All URL fetching goes through netguard.safe_get (public addresses only, every redirect hop checked, the connection pinned to the address that was checked, size and time capped). Do not call httpx directly.
  • The nightly time is in the plist. The launchd agent is static: changing [run].nightly_time needs sb schedule install again (sb doctor warns on a mismatch). Launchd agents cannot read ~/Documents until macOS privacy allows that binary, which only the user can grant.
  • The daily note is a view. It is regenerated from state (source notes and the queue); the only input channel is the user's ticked checkboxes, read before each regeneration. Never make the worker depend on text it wrote earlier in that note. Home.md is partly the user's: only the block between the esbi markers is rewritten.
  • State lives in the vault. .esbi/ holds the queue, the page index and logs. Anything that changes the queue table needs a migration (Queue.__init__ migrates old databases), because the real database lives in users' vaults.
  • Injected defaults bind at definition time. A function that takes an injectable runner as a default argument (launchctl=run_launchctl) must be given it explicitly at the call site, or a test's patch is silently bypassed and the test talks to the real system.
  • A signal raises only where it is safe. Handlers are installed only inside interrupts.handling() (and nothing is installed off the main thread). New code that writes several files must do it inside deferred(), or a Ctrl-C can leave half a note; new code that waits on a model or the network can be wrapped in interruptible(). A try/except Exception is not enough to clean up after an interruption, since Interrupted is a BaseException: use finally, or let run_queue release the item.
  • jsonout.event(kind, /, **fields) takes its kind positionally. A step event has a field called name, and a keyword called name would collide with a parameter of the same name. Keep the /, and never name a parameter after a field an event can carry.
  • Every --json command goes through jsonout. A new field is additive and keeps the contract number; a renamed or removed one is a breaking change that bumps it (and tests/test_json_output.py holds the golden copy of each shape, checked strictly: a key that a command emits and the golden shape does not list fails the test, so a new field has to be written down in the shape, and in JSON output, in the same change). Printing to stdout from a command that has --json breaks the "stdout is JSON only" rule: use stderr for anything human.
  • The proxy setting is per command. netguard.use_environment_proxy is module state that load_config sets from [network] and reset_loaded() puts back to False at the start of each invocation, so the menu or a test that runs several commands in one process cannot carry a proxy setting from one to the next.
  • A clip's doc.text is the stripped text. extract/clip.py removes known page chrome (extract/noise.py) before it builds the ExtractedDoc, so everything after extraction (the content hash, the raw/ snapshot, the chunks, quote checks) sees the stripped text, never the clip as it arrived; that original lives only in raw/inbox/. ExtractedDoc.stripped_lines carries the count into the note's frontmatter. A rule that works on the original clip text has to read raw/inbox/, not doc.text.
  • PDFs: PDFium is not thread-safe, and its y axis points up. The PDF reader (extract/pdf.py, pdf_text.py, pdf_figures.py) opens a document, reads it and closes it in one call, in one thread; PDFium (pypdfium2's engine) does not support concurrent use, so never read two PDFs from parallel threads. Coordinates are PDF points with the origin at the bottom left (Rect is left, bottom, right, top), so a line lower on the page has a smaller baseline, and "below" means a smaller y. PDFium gives characters with a font size and weight and nothing else: paragraphs, headings and table rows are rebuilt by pdf_text.py, and a scan has no characters at all (OCR takes over below 200 characters).
  • PDF tests read committed files. The fixtures are in tests/fixtures/pdf/ (a scan, a locked file, a rotated page, charts, drawn figures, a figure repeated 100 times, a huge image...), written once with a throwaway script, so no PDF library is needed to build them and the reader is tested on files it did not make. Add a case by committing a small PDF, not by generating one in the test.
  • Heading names are data. Note headings come from the language catalogue (lang.py), and readers recognise the headings of every catalogued language. Do not compare against a hard-coded heading.

docs.title: Concepts and glossary
docs.text: The words esbi-cli uses, in plain language. The first part tells the story in order; the second is an A to Z list you can search.

docs.title: The story in one minute
docs.text:
You save things: a link, a PDF, an email, a clip from your browser. Each one becomes an item in the queue. When sb run works through the queue, a language model reads the source and the worker writes a source note in your wiki, plus pages for the concepts and entities it mentions, and links to the pages you already had. The original is kept in raw. Each morning an index note lists what was processed so you can read it and tick it off. Later you can ask the wiki a question and get an answer that cites your notes.

Three layers, as in Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern: raw/ is what you saved and is never edited; wiki/ is what the worker writes and you read (and may edit); SCHEMA.md is the rulebook the model is given.

docs.title: Where the pieces live
docs.text:
vault/
├── inbox/         drop zone: PDFs, clips, images waiting to be picked up
├── raw/           the originals, never edited
├── attachments/   figures copied out of PDFs
├── wiki/
│   ├── sources/   one note per source
│   ├── concepts/  one page per idea
│   ├── entities/  one page per person, organization, tool
│   ├── syntheses/ answers you saved with sb ask --save
│   ├── daily/     one index note per day
│   └── review/    things for you to look at
├── SCHEMA.md      the rules the model is given
├── index.md       catalogue of every page
├── log.md         append-only history
└── .esbi/         the worker's own state (queue, page index, logs)

The full layout is in What lives where.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Ask. sb ask "question": the worker finds the pages that may answer, shows them to a model, and prints the answer with the pages it cites. It answers only from your notes and refuses when it cannot cite one.

Chunk. A piece of a long source, cut at paragraph boundaries (about chunk_chars characters). A source longer than max_source_chars is read chunk by chunk, and the model writes the note from the notes it took on each chunk, never from the raw text.

Clip. A Markdown file made by a browser extension (the Obsidian Web Clipper) or by hand, with title: and source: (the page URL) at the top. The clipped text is the source: the worker does not fetch the page again.

Concept. A page about an idea or technique (wiki/concepts/). It grows by one ## From [[source]] section (## Desde [[source]] in a Spanish vault) for every source that mentions it.

Content hash. A fingerprint of a source's text, kept in the note's frontmatter. The same text arriving under another URL is recognised by it and skipped.

Daily index (or daily note). wiki/daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md: where the day starts. It is rebuilt from the vault's state on every run; the only thing the worker reads back from it is the boxes you ticked. See The daily index.

Edit plan. The JSON the model returns for a source: title, summary, concepts, entities, and so on. The worker validates it against a schema, checks what it claims against the source, and only then writes files. The model never writes a file.

Entity. A page about a proper noun: a person, an organization, a tool (wiki/entities/). An entity whose name does not appear in the source text is dropped, because small models copy names from other pages.

Fallback. A second model named in a [llm.*] section, used when the main model cannot be reached (a spent usage window, a lost login, a server down).

Format 2 note. The current layout of a source note, marked format: 2 in its frontmatter: executive summary, detailed summary, key ideas, glossary, quotes, diagram, figures, connections, open questions. Older notes lack the marker; sb reingest rebuilds them.

Frontmatter. The block of key: value lines between --- lines at the top of a note. The worker keeps type, title, url, kind, status, captured, processed, read, tags, summary, raw, content_hash, format there.

Ingest. Turning one source into notes: extract its text, read it, plan, check, write. sb run ingests the queue; sb ingest does one source immediately.

Inbox. The vault's inbox/ folder. Files dropped there are moved to raw/inbox/ and queued by sb scan (which sb run does first).

Kind. What sort of source it is: article, paper, email or video. email has special privacy rules.

Local model. A model that runs on your own machine (Ollama, LM Studio). The opposite of a model that "sends text out".

Nightly job. A scheduled sb run --if-due (launchd on macOS; on an unsupported system you can try cron) that works through the queue at a time you choose.

Orphan. A page that no other page links to. sb lint lists them.

Private model. [llm.private]: the only model that is allowed to read email. It must run on this machine.

Queue. The list of sources waiting to be ingested, kept in .esbi/queue.sqlite3. A source is queued, processing, done or failed (after three failed attempts). sb status shows the counts.

Raw. raw/: the original of every source, written once and never edited or overwritten. sb reingest rebuilds notes from it.

Read state. A source note is processed when the worker has written it and read when you have ticked it in a daily note and run sb index. It never goes back.

Recall@k and MRR. The two numbers sb eval prints. Recall@k is how often the right page is among the k pages retrieved for a question; MRR (mean reciprocal rank) is how high it ranks (1 for first, 0.5 for second).

Reingest. sb reingest: rebuild source notes from raw/ with the current pipeline, keeping your read ticks, dates and tags. The vault is tagged in git first, so one command undoes it.

Review queue. wiki/review/: notes the worker leaves for you instead of acting on them silently (a possible contradiction, the lint report). They also appear under To review in the daily index.

Run lock. A lock file that makes sure only one sb run or sb reingest works at a time. A crashed run cannot leave it stuck.

SCHEMA.md. The rulebook given to the model on every operation: the layers, the page types, the frontmatter, the link rules. You can read it; changing it changes how the model is told to behave.

Sends text out. A flag on every model, and the heart of the privacy rules. A model "sends text out" when someone else runs it: an API (openai, anthropic), your Claude subscription (claude-cli), your ChatGPT plan (codex-cli), an Ollama or LM Studio server on another machine, or an Ollama -cloud model. A model on your own machine does not. Email is never shown to a model that sends text out. See Safety and privacy.

Source. One thing you saved: a web page, a PDF, an email, a clip, an image. The worker keeps its original in raw/ and writes a source note for it.

Source note. The page the worker writes for a source, in wiki/sources/.

State folder. .esbi/ inside the vault: the queue, the page index, the run history, logs. It is git-ignored except for golden.jsonl (your sb eval questions); the page index is disposable and rebuilt if deleted.

Synthesis. A page in wiki/syntheses/ made from an answer you chose to keep (sb ask --save). It names the pages it came from.

Vault. The folder that holds everything: the Markdown files you read, plus raw/ and the state folder. It is an Obsidian vault, a git repository (when git is installed), and just a folder of text files.

Viewer. The [notes].viewer setting: obsidian (open notes with an obsidian:// link) or none (print paths; use any editor).

Wiki. wiki/: the notes the worker writes and maintains. You read it; you may edit it.

docs.title: Frequently asked questions
docs.text: Short answers, with a link to the page that has the whole story.

docs.title: What does it cost?
docs.text:
The program is free and open source (MIT). What costs money is the model that writes the notes:

  • A local model (Ollama, LM Studio): nothing but electricity.
  • Your ChatGPT plan (codex-cli): the same idea through OpenAI's codex tool, with about 8,500 tokens of overhead per call, so use it for the writing model only.
  • Your Claude subscription: no extra bill, but every call counts against your plan's usage windows. When one is spent the run stops and resumes later.
  • An API key: per token. A source costs roughly 3,000 to 25,000 tokens in the worker's own count: in the example in Getting started, a five-chunk Wikipedia article and a one-page PDF used 27,252 tokens together. A run stops after max_tokens_per_run (300,000 by default), so a mistake cannot run up a large bill. sb bench estimates cost per model once you give it prices (Configuration).

docs.title: How long does a note take?
docs.text: With a small local model on a laptop, 3 to 15 minutes per source; a long paper is on the slow side. That is why the normal way to use it is the nightly job. With your subscription or an API, a three-chunk source took about a minute. Reading an image takes from a few seconds to under a minute per page. Rebuilding 24 notes with sb reingest took about 2.5 hours on an 8 GB Mac. Asking a question takes seconds to a minute or two.

docs.title: Which model should I use?
docs.text: Start with Ollama and llama3.2: free, private, and it runs on an 8 GB Mac. It writes useful but plain notes. If the notes are too thin, move only the writing model ([llm.synthesize]) to your subscription or an API and keep the reading local. qwen3:4b answers questions with better citations but is about ten times slower. To choose with evidence on your own material, run sb bench. See Choose how the notes are written.

docs.title: Is my data private?
docs.text: With a local model, nothing leaves your machine. With a cloud model (an API key, or your Claude or ChatGPT subscription) the text of each source goes to that provider. Email never does: a local model reads it, and cloud models are never shown email pages. The mail password lives in the macOS Keychain. There is no telemetry and no account. See Safety and privacy.

docs.title: Can I edit the notes?
docs.text: Yes: they are yours, plain Markdown. The worker does not overwrite an edit on its own. Two things to know: sb reingest writes a source note again from its original, so edits to its body are lost (the vault is tagged in git first, so you can get them back; tags and your read ticks are kept); and new sources that mention a concept add a ## Desde [[source]] section to that concept's page, leaving your text alone. Never edit between the esbi marker comments in Home.md.

docs.title: What if I delete a note?
docs.text:
Nothing breaks, but things around it notice:

  • A source note. The original stays in raw/. The queue still remembers the source as done, so sb add URL says already known: run sb drop URL first, then sb add URL to make the note again. Links to the deleted note, in concept pages, become broken, and sb lint lists them as broken-link.
  • A concept or entity page. The next source that mentions the idea creates the page again, with only that source's section. Until then, links to it are broken.
  • By mistake. If you use git (recommended), the deletion is a diff and the note is in the history: Back up and restore.

docs.title: Can the notes be in English or another language?
docs.text:
Yes: English (the default) or Spanish, chosen by [notes].language in the config (sb init --language en|es writes it). The setting decides the instruction to the model, the section headings of every note, the daily index, index.md, the lint and benchmark reports and the answers of sb ask. Quotes stay in the source's language, and the sources can be in any language the model reads. The command line and the documentation are always English. Details: Language of the notes.

Another language is a data-only change in one file (a dictionary entry): Add a language. Notes written in a language you no longer use stay as they are, and sb reingest --all rebuilds them in the new one.

A question to sb ask can be in any language; the answer is in the notes' language.

One limit of a vault that holds both languages: search is by words, and rewrite_questions translates a question into the language of [notes].language and English only. After switching a Spanish vault to en, a question in English may not find a Spanish note by keyword. Turn on hybrid search ([llm.embed]), which compares meaning, or rebuild the old notes with sb reingest --all.

Does a small model write good Spanish? Measured with llama3.2 (3B) on four sources, Spanish and English output both came out in the right language on the first try, with no retry; see the numbers in the pull request that added the setting, or run sb bench on your own material. A model that answers in the source's language instead is asked once more, and then kept with a warning.

docs.title: Does it run on Windows or Linux?
docs.text: Not supported for now. macOS is the only supported platform: Linux and Windows (WSL included) are not supported, and nothing is promised there. Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 were tried in containers and the problems found were fixed, so Linux may work (cron instead of launchd, and email capture needs a desktop keyring); WSL and native Windows were not tried. See Other systems.

docs.title: Do I need Obsidian? Do I need git?
docs.text: Neither. Obsidian is only a viewer: any Markdown editor works, and sb export makes a website (Use it without Obsidian). Git gives you history and a backup, and is used if it is installed (Back up and restore).

docs.title: Can I point it at my existing Obsidian vault?
docs.text: It is better not to. The worker adds inbox/, raw/, wiki/, attachments/, SCHEMA.md, index.md and log.md, and rewrites index.md every run, so an index.md of your own would be overwritten. It never changes your existing notes, but sb ask, sb lint and the index only look in wiki/. Use a separate vault: you can open it in Obsidian next to your own, and link from your notes to it.

docs.title: Can I use it on two computers?
docs.text: Not at the same time on one vault. The run lock is a file lock on one machine, so two machines working on a synced folder can step on each other. Use one machine as the worker and read the vault anywhere, or move the vault between machines with git (Move to a new Mac).

docs.title: How good are the notes?
docs.text: Quality tracks the model. A small local model writes useful but unpolished notes; a stronger model writes noticeably better ones. Quotes are always real (they are checked against the source), glossary terms are always in the source, and entities are always named in it. Summaries can still be a little off, connections can be generic, and a diagram can contain an odd edge: treat them as a first draft to read, not as findings. See How a note is made and What the worker repairs.

docs.title: Where do I report a bug or ask for something?
docs.text: GitHub Issues. Paste the output of sb doctor. Security problems go through private reporting: see Safety and privacy.

docs.title: How a note is made
docs.text: A source note is written so that you can skip the original: read the note, know what the source says, decide whether it deserves your time.

docs.title: What a note looks like
docs.text:
You save a link or a paper. A few minutes later there is a note like this (abridged, from a Wikipedia article, written by llama3.2 on a laptop):

## Executive summary
The Zettelkasten is a method of note-taking and knowledge management developed by Niklas Luhmann,
which involves creating a network of interconnected notes and ideas. It emphasizes the importance of
linking and connecting ideas, rather than simply collecting or storing them.

## Key ideas
- **The Zettelkasten system emphasizes the use of index cards to organize and connect ideas.** This
  approach allows users to create a network of interconnected notes, rather than a linear sequence of thoughts.

## Key terms
- **Zettelkasten**: A system of note-taking and personal knowledge management that consists of small
  items of information stored on paper slips or cards.

## Key quotes
> "Every one admits nowadays that it is advisable to collect materials on separate cards or slips of paper."

## Concepts
- [[Index card file]]

The language is a setting, [notes].language (default en). With es the same kind of note reads like this (abridged, from a paper on the Transformer, written by an earlier version of the pipeline):

## Resumen ejecutivo
El artículo describe el modelo Transformer, que usa mecanismos de atención para la
traducción de secuencias y supera a los modelos publicados en calidad y coste de entrenamiento.

## Ideas clave
- **El Transformer se basa exclusivamente en atención.** Es una alternativa a los modelos
  recurrentes y convolucionales, dominantes hasta entonces.

## Términos clave
- **Self-attention**: Un mecanismo que relaciona posiciones de una secuencia para calcular su representación.

## Frases clave
> "We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely"

Quotes always stay in the language of the source. Section headings, the daily index and the other text the program writes follow the setting; see Language of the notes.

Quotes are checked against the source word for word, glossary terms must appear in it, diagrams are drawn by code, and PDF figures are copied next to the note. The model never touches your files: it only returns JSON that the program validates and then writes.

docs.title: How it is made
docs.text:
Images and scanned PDFs first. With [llm.ocr] set, a vision model reads the text printed in an image (or in each page of a PDF that has no text layer, up to ocr_max_pages), and that text is the source from here on: everything below, including the checks that quotes appear verbatim, is against what the OCR model read. The picture itself is kept in raw/ and shown in the note.

The language. The instructions to the model are in English for every output language: they name the language to write in (Write ALL text in Spanish) and the request for the note repeats it after the source, where a small model listens. If the answer comes back in the wrong language the worker asks once more, and keeps the second answer with a warning if it is still wrong. A language the program has no word list for is never judged.

The steps:

  1. The fence. Every prompt that carries a source puts it between tags (<source>, <chunk>...), and first makes any look-alike tag or chat marker inside the source inert (fence.py), so a source cannot close the tag and start giving orders in the prompt's own voice. The title and URL that go into an instruction are quoted for the same reason.
  2. Reading. A source that fits in max_source_chars goes to the model whole. A longer one (most papers) is cut into chunks at paragraph boundaries; the references section is dropped. The reading model (llm.summarize) takes notes on every chunk, however many there are: points, defined terms, verbatim quotes, and relations between concepts. A chunk it cannot read is read again in two halves, which a small model often manages; only a chunk that stays unreadable is skipped, with a warning, not a failure. A source of more chunks than max_chunks has the notes of each group of five chunks merged into a section note, level by level, until max_chunks or fewer remain, and the next step works from those (see Long sources). A cap on the model calls for one source (max_calls_per_source) keeps the cost bounded; when it stops the reading early the note says so (below).
  3. Synthesis. The synthesis model (llm.synthesize, or the same one) receives the notes, not the raw text, and writes the digest below. The detailed summary is asked for as 3 to 4 short paragraphs and 4 to 6 key ideas: a list is something a small model can be held to, where one long string ran on until it hit its limit.
  4. Connections. A separate call shows the model the pages you already have (with their one-line summaries) and asks how the new source relates to them, with the reason. It is a separate call on purpose: showing a small model existing pages while it summarizes makes it copy their wording into the new note.
  5. Scrub, checks, then writing. First everything the model wrote is scrubbed as plain prose (scrub.py): no HTML, no image syntax, no control characters; a link or address stays only if the source contains it; a [[link]] stays only if the page exists and a note on this side of the email line may point at it. The run says how many addresses were removed. Then the worker verifies before it writes: quotes must appear verbatim in the source, glossary terms and entities must appear in the source text, invented links are dropped, glossary trivia (duplicates, generic words such as "data", entries that say they have no definition, a lone letter) is dropped, and the diagram is drawn by code from the extracted relations (so it is always valid Mermaid), keeping only relations whose two ends appear in the source or in the note.
  6. Later, on the concept pages. Once a concept or entity page has several sources, a short ## Summary on top of its per-source sections can be written from them: see Consolidated summaries. It is a separate step, off in the nightly run by default.

What the note contains (sections with nothing to say are left out; the table gives the English heading and, in brackets, the Spanish one):

Section What it is Not read (a warning callout under the title, only when it applies) > [!warning] Not read: 12 of 52 parts of the source (the last 23% of the text, starting at "...") because the limit of 60 model calls per source ([run].max_calls_per_source) was reached. (No leído: ... in a Spanish note). Present only when the call cap stopped the reading before the end of a very long source: how many parts and what share of the text were left out, and where they start Executive summary (Resumen ejecutivo) The 2-4 sentence answer to "what is this and why does it matter" Detailed summary (Resumen detallado) The abstract, in 3 to 4 paragraphs: the argument in order, with the data that supports it Key ideas (Ideas clave) 4 to 6 ideas, each with what follows from it (or plain key points if the model gave none) Key terms (Términos clave) A glossary of terms the source defines, linked to your concept pages Key quotes (Frases clave) Verbatim quotes worth keeping Diagram (Diagrama) A Mermaid concept map of the relations found Figures (Figuras) PDF figures (up to 8, captioned ones first) copied into attachments/; for web pages, images are linked, not downloaded Connections to your wiki (Conexiones con tu wiki) Pages you already have this relates to, with the relation and why Open questions (Preguntas abiertas) What the source leaves unanswered Concepts / Entities / Related (Conceptos, Entidades, Relacionado) Links to the pages the note created or updated

docs.title: PDFs
docs.text:
A PDF has no paragraphs, headings or tables of its own: it is characters placed on pages, each with a font size and weight. The worker (extract/pdf_text.py, on PDFium) turns them into plain Markdown the model can read:

  • Lines are reflowed into paragraphs by the gaps between lines and by indents. A hyphen at the end of a line is dropped inside a word (en-ables becomes enables) and kept in a compound (feed-forward). The test uses the document's own vocabulary, but not the halves of words that a line break cut (plicative is no word of the paper, so it cannot make multi look like one). The hyphen goes when the joined word is a word of the document, or a word of it with an ending (leverage gives leveraged, omit gives omitted); it stays when the first half is a short joining word (of, in, non...) or a word of the document, usually a long one (sequence-aligned, mixture-of-experts).
  • Running headers, footers and page numbers (a line repeated in the top or bottom margin of at least three pages) are dropped. A References heading is kept as a heading, which is what lets the reader drop the references section later.
  • Headings are found by font size, weight and numbering: a short line (at most 100 characters, not ending in a comma, period or semicolon) that is at least 12% bigger than the body text, or that is bold and starts with a number or one of A., Abstract, Appendix. Numbered ones take their level from the number (1 Introduction is ##, 3.1 Method is ###); the others rank by size. A document can have only so many headings: the cap is the larger of 40 and 8 per page, and when a file has more heading-like lines than that (the labels of a chart set in big type), the numbered ones and the biggest ones are kept and the rest become plain text. Before, more than 200 such lines switched heading detection off for the whole file.
  • Tables are not Markdown tables. A line that is mostly numbers stays one row per line with its numbers intact (Base 65 27.3 3.3); the worker does not guess columns.
  • Text inside images and charts is dropped: text over a picture, and three kinds of chart text. A run of at least 12 label-like lines (axes, legends, bar values) goes. A short line that the document repeats 8 times or more goes too: prose does not repeat a line, and a figure drawn in layers can repeat its labels by the hundred (one test paper had its labels printed 80 times and, before this rule, came out with more than twice the text it has). And short lines packed into a small region of a page (40 or more within about 150 points) are the text of a chart, not of a page, so they go, with the neighbouring cells. A symbol inside a line of prose stays: the V of where V is, or a superscript on the row of its text, is not a label, even when the paper repeats it. Emphasis markers (**, _x_) are not written, so a quote the model copies matches the PDF word for word more often.
  • Figures (extract/pdf_figures.py) are embedded images of a reasonable size, and also a vector drawing (a diagram, a flow chart) that has a Figure N caption next to it. The panels under one caption are one figure: parts up to 120 points apart join, for drawings and for pictures alike, so the left panel of a two-panel figure or the top row of a six-panel one is no longer lost. A table of numbers is not a panel, a figure keeps out of the column of another caption beside it (a table drawn next to a figure, and its text, are not taken into the figure), and the caption of another figure ends the search upwards, so two stacked figures stay two. A PDF printed several pages to a sheet (2 pages per sheet, a handout, a booklet) places each page as a form, and its pictures and drawings are found where the sheet puts them (two identical copies are kept once). At most 8 per PDF, captioned ones first, rendered at 150 dpi and no more than 3,000 pixels a side. A scanned page is rendered at 130 dpi for OCR.

Compared with the engine used before (PyMuPDF with a layout model), this one needs about 8 MB instead of 214 MB, reads a paper of 15 to 50 pages in about a second or less instead of 8 to 60 seconds, and uses about a third of the memory (measured on 10 papers of 8 to 51 pages). The price is the table and chart behaviour above. A note made from an older version is rebuilt from the new text with sb reingest (the PDF is read again from raw/).

Known limits of the PDF reader: the thresholds above (8 repeats, 40 short lines, 120 points, the heading cap) were tuned on a small corpus of test papers, about ten, so a layout unlike them can still go wrong in either direction. The hyphen rule is a heuristic on the document's own vocabulary: a compound whose first half is short and whose second half is not a word of the paper (gpt-researcher) can be joined into one word, and a broken word whose long first half is itself a word keeps its hyphen (multi-plicative).

Known limits of notes in general: a source that needs more than about 45 chunks is read only as far as max_calls_per_source allows, and the note discloses the unread tail (raise the cap for books; a long source costs about two to three times the tokens and time it did when it was sampled); a page that is mostly a list of links (a GitHub README of links) has little to summarize; quality tracks the synthesis model.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
you save things                 the worker (sb run)                        you read
 ───────────────                 ──────────────────                        ────────
 Web Clipper → inbox/  ┐
 forwarded email        ├─►  queue ─► fetch & extract ─► LLM writes a  ─►  wiki/ notes + index.md + log.md
 an older notes folder ┘    (SQLite)  (web, PDF, note)   JSON edit plan     wiki/daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md  ◄── start here

Three layers, as in Karpathy's design:

  • raw/: the original of every source, never edited.
  • wiki/: notes written and maintained by the worker: one source note per source, plus concept, entity and synthesis pages that grow as more sources arrive. You read it in Obsidian; the worker writes it.
  • SCHEMA.md: the conventions the model is given on every run.

Design rules worth knowing:

  • The model never touches your files. It only returns a JSON "edit plan". The worker validates the plan (drops invented links, rejects wrong-language or malformed output, retries once) and only then writes.
  • Everything is a git commit in the vault repo (when git is installed; it is optional), one per ingested source, so any change can be reviewed or reverted.
  • Risky things go to review, not to the wiki: contradictions and lint findings become notes under wiki/review/. Nothing is merged or deleted silently.
  • It works with small local models (Ollama) and with cloud models through the same interface.

docs.text: How esbi-cli works inside, and why it is built this way. For using it, read Getting started, How do I...? and the command reference. For what is unfinished, read Known limits below.

docs.title: The idea in one paragraph
docs.text: The pattern is Karpathy's LLM Wiki: raw/ holds the originals and is never edited; wiki/ holds notes the worker writes and maintains; SCHEMA.md holds the conventions the model is given. A Python worker does the file work. A language model only ever returns JSON, which the worker validates and then applies. The model never touches a file and never calls a tool, so it works with small local models.

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph capture
    A[inbox/ clips and PDFs] --> Q
    B[email via IMAP] --> A
    C[sb add / legacy import] --> Q
  end
  Q[(queue, SQLite)] --> R[run_queue]
  R --> X[extract: web, PDF, clip]
  X --> S[save_raw -> raw/]
  X --> CH[split_chunks]
  CH --> RD[read_chunks: notes per chunk]
  RD --> PL[make_plan: core plan]
  PL --> DG[make_digest: abstract and ideas]
  RD --> AG[aggregate: terms, quotes, relations]
  PL --> CN[connect: links to existing pages]
  DG --> AP[apply_plan]
  AG --> AP
  CN --> AP
  AP --> W[wiki/ notes + attachments/]
  W --> G[git commit in the vault]
  W --> IDX[index.md, log.md, daily note]

One source, step by step (ingest/pipeline.py):

  1. Fence (fence.py): every prompt that carries untrusted text (the source, a chunk, a title, the existing pages, the question) passes it through fence_safe first: a look-alike of the tags the prompt builders open (<source>, <chunk>, <chunk_notes>, <section_notes>, <existing_pages>...) or a chat marker (<|...|>, <<SYS>>, [INST]) is turned into something inert, and titles and URLs are quoted with json.dumps so they cannot add lines to the instructions. It stops a source from forging structure; it does not make a model ignore what the source asks.
  2. Extract (extract/): a URL becomes text with trafilatura (and up to five article image links); a PDF becomes plain Markdown from PDFium's characters (extract/pdf_text.py: paragraphs, headings by font size, weight and numbering, table rows one per line) plus up to eight figures, images and captioned vector drawings (extract/pdf_figures.py); a Web Clipper note is read from its own body, after the known page chrome of five sites (GitHub, LinkedIn, X, Reddit, YouTube) has been removed whole line by whole line (extract/noise.py; the count goes to stripped_lines). Every URL the worker fetches itself goes through netguard.safe_get: http(s) only, public addresses only, every redirect re-checked.
  3. Deduplicate: by URL and by a hash of the text. A duplicate is skipped with no model call.
  4. Read (ingest/chunks.py, ingest/read.py): a source longer than max_source_chars is cut into chunks at paragraph boundaries and the references section is dropped. The reading model takes notes on every chunk: points, terms, verbatim quotes, relations. A source of more than max_chunks chunks then has those notes merged into section notes (ingest/mapreduce.py, see Long sources). A chunk it cannot read twice is read again in two halves; only when both halves fail too is it skipped with a warning (Only half of chunk 2 of 5 could be read. when one of them works).
  5. Retrieve (ingest/retrieve.py, index.py): the worker finds existing pages that may relate to this source with SQLite full-text search (FTS5) over a persistent index that is kept in step with the files by their size and modification time. Page lookups by name and source lookups by URL or hash use the same index.
  6. Plan (ingest/plan.py): the writing model gets the notes (not the raw text) and the titles of candidate pages, and returns a core plan: title, one-liner, summary, key points, tags, concepts, entities.
  7. Digest (ingest/digest.py): a second, small call writes the detailed summary, key ideas and open questions. The detailed summary is a list of 3 to 4 paragraphs (paragraphs) and the key ideas are 4 to 6 short ones, because a list is something a small model's grammar can bound and one long string was not (the first try failed about one time in four with llama3.2; it is now about one in twenty-five). The retry names the problem and asks for less. Terms, quotes and diagram relations are not asked of the model again: code merges what the chunk notes already contain.
  8. Connect (ingest/connect.py): a third call is shown the existing pages with their one-liners and says how the new source relates to them, with the reason.
  9. Scrub, then apply (scrub.py, ingest/apply.py): apply_plan first walks the whole plan and passes every string the model wrote through scrub (plain prose: no HTML, no image syntax, no control characters; a Markdown link or address only if the source contains it; a [[link]] only to an existing page that this side of the email line may point at), counting the addresses it cut (ApplyResult.stripped_addresses). Quotes and glossary terms are not scrubbed: they are checked word for word against the source instead. apply_plan is the only module that writes wiki pages. It checks every claim before writing (see "Trust model") and then writes the source note, creates or extends concept and entity pages, writes figures into attachments/, and records what it did. It reports what it dropped in ApplyResult (unsupported_terms, trivial_terms, dropped_edges, unsupported_entities). The writing is done inside interrupts.deferred(), so a signal waits for the note to be whole.
  10. Consolidate (ingest/consolidate.py, optional): for the concept and entity pages this source touched that now have enough sources, a ## Summary is written on top of their per-source sections, up to [run].max_consolidations_per_run (0 by default). sb consolidate does the same on demand.
  11. Report (report/): index.md, log.md, and the daily note are regenerated. The vault is committed to git.

docs.title: Long sources
docs.text:
A source of at most max_chunks chunks (16 of 8,000 characters by default) is read one call per chunk and goes to the plan as it is, exactly as always. A longer one (a book, a 60,000-word document) used to be sampled, so the note was about its first third. Now it is read by a bounded map-reduce (ingest/mapreduce.py):

  1. Map. Every chunk gets its own notes (points, terms, quotes, relations), with the same retries and the same split into halves as before.
  2. Reduce. The notes of each group of 5 chunks are merged by the model into one section note, level by level, until at most max_chunks notes remain. A group of one passes up unchanged. The plan, the detailed summary and the connections are written from those notes, never from the raw text, so no prompt outgrows the model's context window (a merge prompt carries at most 12,000 characters of notes).
  3. The finale reserves 7 calls. Before each chunk the worker checks that the calls left cover the merges the notes read so far will need plus the 7 calls the plan (2 attempts), the detailed summary (3) and the connections (2) can take. When they do not, reading stops there.

What the model is allowed to do in a merge is small. It rewrites only the points of a section (3 to 8 sentences). The terms, quotes and relations of every chunk are carried over by code (a spread of them per section), never by the model, so nothing it could invent reaches the note, and they are still checked against the source at the end like any other. If a merge fails (invalid twice, too slow, no calls left), code merges the points and the run warns Section 2 was merged without the model (...).

The call cap. [run].max_calls_per_source (60, minimum 12) counts every model call of one source, retries and halves included; a call that fails was still paid for. When it stops the reading early, the source is not dropped: the note starts, under its title, with a warning callout saying how many parts and what share of the text were not read and where the unread part starts (> [!warning] Not read: 12 of 52 parts of the source (the last 23% of the text, starting at "...") because the limit of 60 model calls per source ([run].max_calls_per_source) was reached., No leído: ... in a Spanish note), and the run prints the same as a warning. Nothing is dropped silently. A source that needs more than about 45 chunks (about 45 chunks, roughly 350,000 characters at the default chunk size, fewer when chunks need retries) is read only as far as the cap allows: raise the cap for books. A source of 40 chunks takes about 55 calls, which is two to three times the model calls (so, roughly, the tokens and the time) of the old sampling, which made 16 chunk calls and the finale.

The progress lines and sb run --json show the new step as merging section 2 of 8 ({"event":"step","name":"merging section","index":2,"total":8}), like the chunk step.

docs.title: Design decisions, and why
docs.text:
The model returns JSON, the worker writes files. Small local models cannot be trusted with file tools, but they can fill a schema. The schema (llm/schemas.py, pydantic) is the contract, and it is also what the model is given as a JSON schema, so the model's decoder is constrained to it. Every list in the schema has a maxItems: measured on a 3B model, without it a chunk's notes ran away in 3 of 4 cases.

Reading is separate from writing. A shallow summary was a reading problem: the model saw only the first 12k characters of sources whose median is 47k. Long sources are read in full, in chunks, by a cheap model; the writing model works from the notes. They can be two different models ([llm.summarize] reads, [llm.synthesize] writes) or the same one with different limits.

One job per model call. One giant plan left the abstract empty. The core plan, the digest and the connections are three small calls; code does the merging that needs no model. Connections are a separate call because showing a small model existing pages while it summarizes makes it copy their wording into the new note.

Trust model: the worker checks what the model claims.

Claim Check A quote Must appear verbatim in the source (ignoring case and accents) A glossary term Must appear in the source text (markup and spaces around it are stripped). Dropped as trivia: a duplicate (ignoring case, accents and punctuation, and an acronym in either letter order such as IA and AI), a generic word (data, system: a per-language list, generic_terms), a one-letter term (a formula symbol), a definition that says it has none (not defined in the text: a per-language pattern, disclaimers) An entity (person, tool, company) Its name or an alias must appear in the source text A link to a page Must resolve to a real page, or it is dropped An address (Markdown link or bare URL) or an image Kept only if the exact address is in the source; otherwise removed and counted. Image syntax and HTML are never kept A name for a concept, entity or alias Not Home, index, log, lint, SCHEMA or a date, and an alias must not already name another page A contradiction Only on a page on the same side of the email line as the source A concept named like a source Skipped: Obsidian resolves [[links]] by filename across folders, so it would be ambiguous The language The notes' language ([notes].language), with one retry; a second failure is accepted and reported. The check is a count of common words, so a language without a word list is never judged A one-line summary that is a URL, a label or the title Replaced by the first sentence of the summary The concept diagram Drawn by code from the extracted relations, so the Mermaid syntax is always valid. A relation whose end is neither in the source nor a concept, entity, term or alias of the note (translated or inflected is fine) is dropped, and the run says how many (Dropped 2 diagram edges: an end was not in the source or the note.). The prompts ask for relation ends as names of one to four words, not sentences; with fewer than two relations left the map is left out A consolidated summary Built only from the page's own sections. 80 to 900 characters, no links, URLs or HTML, the notes' language, and no quote, number or capitalised name that the sections do not contain. One retry; a second failure goes to wiki/review/ and the page stays as it was

Risky changes go to review, never silently. Contradictions and lint findings become notes under wiki/review/. The worker deletes nothing of yours. Contradiction flagging is off by default because small models flag tenuous ones.

A model timeout is not "the model is down". LLMTimeout fails one chunk or one source and the run goes on. Only a real connection failure stops a run, and then nothing is counted against the sources.

An interruption is not a failure either. Ctrl-C or SIGTERM puts the source being read back in the queue with no attempt counted, and a note is never cut in half (deferred() makes a signal wait until the note and its pages are written). Before this, three interruptions parked a perfectly good source. The run exits 130 or 143, and the nightly job does not count an interrupted run as that night's run.

The daily note is a view, not a document. It is regenerated from state (source frontmatter plus the queue) on every run. The only thing read back from it is your - [x] ticks, before each regeneration. The worker never depends on text it wrote earlier in that note.

Idempotent by default. The same link twice is one queue item (tracking parameters, case and trailing slash are normalized). The same PDF twice is recognized by its bytes. A different PDF with the same file name is kept as name (2).pdf. raw/ is never overwritten.

Scheduling uses the calendar, not an interval. The nightly job is a launchd StartCalendarInterval at [run].nightly_time (default 03:00), which launchd runs at the next wake if the Mac was asleep. An hourly interval and run-at-load are only a retry net, because launchd drops interval ticks that fall while the Mac sleeps. --if-due makes the job do real work once per day, plus one more batch per hourly tick while sources are queued, whatever ended the last batch (a source, token or USD limit, or an empty queue that filled again; not an outage or an interruption, which wait for the next nightly boundary), up to [run].max_batches_per_day scheduled batches since the nightly boundary (runlog.is_due: runs stopped by an outage or an interruption, and manual runs, are not counted). The run is wrapped in caffeinate -i.

Social posts and YouTube are captured by hand. Through the Obsidian Web Clipper; the worker does not scrape. The clipped text is the source.

docs.title: sb reingest: how a rebuild stays safe
docs.text:
1. Commit the vault and tag it pre-reingest-<date> (an existing tag means a resumed run, and the first tag is the true "before").
  2. For each note not yet at format: 2 (or matching the titles given): read its original from raw/ (a PDF is re-extracted, so figures come back).
  3. Run the normal pipeline with the old title (so existing [[links]] stay valid) and the old raw path.
  4. Only once the new plan exists, before_write removes what the old note added elsewhere: its ## From [[note]] sections in concept pages (in any language the vault was written in), and any concept page nobody else cites. A model failure before that point leaves the old note untouched.
  5. Restore status, read, captured, content_hash; merge tags; mark format: 2; commit.

Because the marker is the note's own frontmatter, an interrupted rebuild resumes by running the command again.
